body: THE GOOD NUMBER: a payments company growing 30%+ with high margins and a large cash pile, in the DAX, audited by EY for a decade. WHY IT LIED: about half of profits came through third-party acquirers (TPAs) in Asia that Wirecard did not own and that auditors could not see directly; EUR 1.9 bn of cash was said to sit in Philippine trustee accounts. On 18 Jun 2020 EY could not confirm it, on 22 Jun the company said it probably did not exist; insolvency 25 Jun 2020; shares -98%. TELLS: (1) margin and growth far above listed payment peers with lower take-rates in a competitive industry; (2) profits concentrated in an opaque, outsourced segment; (3) operating cash flow much weaker than EBITDA once customer-fund movements were removed; rising receivables; (4) expensive acquisitions in India/Asia paid to obscure funds; (5) the company and regulator (BaFin short-selling ban, complaints against FT journalists) attacked critics instead of producing evidence. TEST: insist that cash is held in the company's own name at a known bank; check whether the profitable segment is the same one you can verify; strip customer/merchant funds out of CFO. LESSON: high quality numbers that live in places you cannot audit are not high quality.

data.good_number: fast revenue/EBITDA growth, ~25-30% EBITDA margins [approx], DAX member, EY audit, EUR 1.9 bn cash
data.test_that_catches_it: where do profits come from (segment you can audit?); cash held by trustees/escrow; CFO ex customer funds vs EBITDA
data.why_misleading: profits came from Asian 'third-party acquirers' it did not control; the cash 'in trustee accounts' did not exist

title: Hidden trap: Wirecard's fintech growth, margins and EUR 1.9 bn cash
